title: Tamsin and the Lantern
premise: In 1747 Lisbon, mapmaker's apprentice Paloma Almeida inherits her dead master's forbidden atlas—a survey of the crown's hidden debts and displaced villages—just as royal orders demand every map be surrendered and burned. When census taker Tamsin Reyes asks one question too many about a village that officially never existed, he is pulled into her flight, becoming both liability and unlikely ally. Together they smuggle the atlas past three checkpoints toward a printer's exile ship, discovering that memory itself is contraband. The book ends with the atlas printed and scattered like seeds while Paloma, choosing exile over safety, lights the lantern that guided her master—and now guides everyone who reads what they saved.
about_author: Zephyrine Crane is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing confiscated maps in Iberian municipal collections before turning to fiction. She writes historical novels about the people history tried to erase, one document at a time.

chapters.title: The Weight of Paper
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. In her dead master's workshop, Paloma finishes inking the final plate of his secret atlas while royal criers announce that all unregistered maps must be surrendered within the week. She measures her life in what can be carried. Emotional beat: grief hardening into resolve.

chapters.title: One Question Too Many
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. Census taker Tamsin Reyes interviews households near the river and finds a widow who insists she lives in Vila Serena—a village struck from every record he carries. His superiors dismiss him; his own ledger begins to feel like a lie. Emotional beat: professional certainty cracking into doubt.

chapters.title: What the Master Died For
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. A crown inspector ransacks the workshop; Paloma hides the atlas plates inside a hollowed lantern frame her master built for exactly this purpose. She flees to the docks, where Tamsin, following the widow's trail, catches her loading it—and must choose whether to report her. Emotional beat: fear sharpened by recognition.

chapters.title: An Unlikely Accomplice
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Tamsin shows Paloma the erased villages in his own census ledgers; two records, two lies, one truth between them. They form an uneasy pact: he knows the checkpoints' procedures, she knows the routes only a mapmaker could read. Emotional beat: wary trust kindling.

chapters.title: First Checkpoint: The Alfama Gate
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Disguised as a funeral procession carrying the lantern as a grave-goods chest, they pass the first checkpoint—but a guard recognizes Tamsin and lets them through with a look that promises betrayal. Emotional beat: relief shadowed by dread.

chapters.title: The Cartographer's Daughter
chapters.summary: Tamsin's POV. They shelter with Marisol, her master's estranged daughter, who reveals her father didn't die of illness—he was interrogated, and someone informed on him. Tamsin realizes the informant may sit above his own office. Emotional beat: the personal cost of power's corruption made flesh.

chapters.title: Second Checkpoint: The Bridge of Boats
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. At the river crossing, soldiers burn confiscated books on the bank; the informer from chapter five waits among them. Marisol creates a diversion that costs her freedom so the pair can cross. Emotional beat: sacrifice transforming guilt into obligation.

chapters.title: Everything That Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Hiding in a salt cellar, Paloma and Tamsin argue over abandoning the heaviest plates to move faster; she refuses, insisting memory cannot be measured by weight. He confesses his census work helped erase Vila Serena. Emotional beat: rupture, then forgiveness as shared purpose.

chapters.title: Third Checkpoint: The Printer's Door
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The final checkpoint is the print shop itself, already surrounded. Tamsin walks in openly, offering himself and his ledgers as evidence to buy Paloma time to carry the lantern through the cellar to the exile ship's waiting printer. Emotional beat: terror transfigured into courage.

chapters.title: The Lantern Lit
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, epilogue-like. From the ship's deck she watches Tamsin marched away but alive—their testimony too public to quietly disappear—and holds the first printed copy of the atlas as copies scatter across Europe. She lights the lantern at the rail. Emotional beat: belonging found not in place, but in purpose carried forward.
